questions.question: How does React Context work and when should you use it vs prop drilling?
questions.title: Usecontext Basics
questions.direct_answer: Context avoids prop drilling by making data available to an entire subtree without passing it through intermediate components. createContext() makes a channel; the Provider's `value` prop sets it; useContext reads it in any descendant. Use for genuinely global, low-frequency data: themes, auth/current-user, locale. Don't use for high-frequency data (every-keystroke state re-renders ALL consumers) or as a general state manager — colocate state or use a state library when updates are frequent.

sections.title: Interview Answer
Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    P[Provider value=...memoized...] --> C1[deep child A]
    P --> C2[deep child B]
    P --> C3[deep child C — no props drilled]
    V[value changes by ref] --> R[ALL consumers re-render]
    S[split: data ctx + setter ctx] --> T[setter-only consumers skip re-render]
    subgraph avoid-when
        H[high-frequency state in context] --> X[every-keystroke app re-render]
    end
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The re-render contract (the mechanism to articulate): context propagation bypasses the normal parent→child render flow. A consumer re-renders when the nearest Provider's value CHANGES BY REFERENCE (Object.is — verified: a literal {…} is new every render; a useMemo value stays stable). memo() on the consumer changes NOTHING for context updates — memo only gates prop-driven renders; context subscription is a separate channel. This is the design: context is a broadcast that can't be intercepted, which is exactly right for theme/user (everyone must update) and exactly wrong for fine-grained state.

The split-context pattern (the production fix for the frequency problem): split the data and its setters into separate contexts — a component that only dispatches (a theme-toggle button) reads the SETTER context (which never changes value) and never re-renders when the theme flips; only components reading the theme context re-render. Libraries formalize this: React Redux's connect/useSelector subscribe to specific slices with store change events instead of context values, which is why selectors re-render only their slices.

The composition rules (the completeness layer): multiple Providers of the same context nest — the NEAREST ancestor wins (shadowing, like variable scope). The default value (createContext's argument) applies only when NO provider exists above the consumer — a provider with value={undefined} does NOT fall back to the default, a subtle bug. And consuming context in a plain function requires the useContext hook (or the render-props Consumer form); class components read it via static contextType — worth knowing for legacy codebases.
